title: Inside the Head of Your Opponent
text:
In 2008 Adam Galinsky, William Maddux, Debra Gilin and Judith White compared two ways of focusing on the other side in a negotiation. Perspective taking means thinking about what the other person wants and why, a mainly mental exercise. Empathy means feeling for the other person and connecting emotionally.

In one study, MBA students negotiated the sale of a gas station. The buyer's highest possible offer was lower than the seller's lowest acceptable price, so a simple deal on price was impossible. But the case contained hidden interests: the seller needed money for a trip and wanted a job afterwards, and the buyer needed someone to run the station. A creative deal, a lower price plus employment, could satisfy both. Before negotiating, buyers were asked either to imagine what the seller was thinking, to imagine what the seller was feeling, or were given no special instructions.

Buyers who took the seller's perspective were the most likely to discover the creative deal. Those who focused on the seller's feelings did better than the control group but not as well. In another study, about a job contract with several issues, perspective takers created more total value and also claimed more of it for themselves, while empathizers sometimes gave too much away.

The authors concluded that in negotiations it pays more to get inside the other side's head than inside their heart, though empathy has its own uses in building relationships.
lesson: Before a negotiation, take time to work out what the other side really needs and why. Understanding their interests reveals deals that a simple tug of war over price would miss.
people: Adam Galinsky, William Maddux, Debra Gilin, Judith White
source: Galinsky, A. D., Maddux, W. W., Gilin, D., and White, J. B. (2008). Why it pays to get inside the head of your opponent: The differential effects of perspective taking and empathy in negotiations. Psychological Science, 19(4), 378-384.
